title: The Best Way to Handle Board Pushback? See It Coming.
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell argues that CEOs who feel their board is against them often skip the one thing that would help most: rehearsing the meeting. He cites Spencer Stuart data showing that only 37 percent of CEOs say their board has their back, against 47 percent of directors who believe it does. Using comedians as a model, he explains that apparently spontaneous performances come from testing and tweaking material, and he suggests CEOs practise important board discussions with someone who will play devil's advocate. He adds an improv mindset, the 'yes, and' principle, so a pointed question is treated as information rather than a threat. He closes by recommending a Board-CEO Operating Agreement, noting that CEOs who explicitly discussed expected support were far more likely to feel supported. The piece includes a brief plug for the author's own AI rehearsal product.
points: A CEO should not discover how the board will react to a key message during the presentation, because anticipation and scenario modelling prevent most of the blindsiding.
Rehearsing with a candid devil's advocate, such as a chief of staff, mentor or experienced CEO, exposes the weakest parts of a plan before directors do.
Treating tough questions with an improv 'yes, and' openness signals sound judgment better than a polished pitch that turns defensive.
Each director brings different experiences and priorities, so a plan should be tested against the likely lenses of skepticism in the room.
An explicit Board-CEO Operating Agreement about decision rights and expected support raised the share of CEOs who felt backed from 50 to 68 percent.
quotes: The lesson is that CEOs shouldn’t be discovering how the board will react to a key message as they are presenting it. A bit of anticipation, preparation, and scenario modeling goes a long, long way.

Every director arrives at your conference table with a different set of experiences, priorities, and mental models. One may have lived through a disastrous acquisition and consequently view your growth plan through a skeptical lens.

Board members are looking for evidence of sound judgment. A CEO who can discuss the risks candidly, entertain alternative scenarios, and still articulate a clear recommendation does far more to build confidence than one who delivers a polished sales pitch and becomes defensive when questioned.
Have them challenge the weakest parts of your plan, question your evidence, and raise the objections you least want to hear.
The idea is to do the stumbling and revising before the actual meeting, so you’re better equipped to think on your feet when it counts.

The Spencer Stuart research I mentioned earlier found that 68% of CEOs who had explicitly discussed with their boards the support and input they should expect felt effectively supported. Among those who hadn’t had those conversations, the figure was just 50%.
